newsitem.title: USA: Gay marriages in Hawaii legalized in landmark ruling.
newsitem.headline: Gay marriages in Hawaii legalized in landmark ruling.

text.p: A judge in Hawaii ruled on Tuesday that same-sex marriages are legal, making the state the first in America to recognise that gay and lesbian couples are entitled to the same privileges as heterosexual married couples.

In his ruling, Hawaii Circuit Court Judge Kevin Chang found that the Hawaiian state government had failed to establish a "compelling state interest" to justify the prohibition against same-sex marriages.
Dan Foley, a lawyer for three same-sex couples who sued the state in the landmark case, told reporters, "I couldn't have gotten more, we got 100 percent."

Hawaii's Deputy Attorney General, Rick Eichor, told reporters he would file for a stay of Chang's order to give him time to study the judge's ruling, and if that was not granted he would make an automatic appeal to the state's Supreme Court.

The legal manoeuvring made it unclear when the first same-sex marriage would take place on the island state, but Eichor said wryly he expected "an increase in our tourism, at least tremporarily," as couples flock to what could become the gay marriage capital of the world.

Foley first filed suit in 1990 on behalf of the three couples -- two of which are lesbian -- and in 1993 the Hawaiian Supreme Court ordered attorneys for the state to show "compelling" reasons why state discrimination against gay marriages was justified.

One of the plaintiffs in the landmark case, Nina Baehr, told a news conference in New York after the decision, "People have told us we would never get this far in the courts, but when we heard the news there were tears in my eyes. I thought I would cry if we lost, but we cried for winning."
She and Genora Dancel, both aged 36, hugged each other for a long time after the decision came down "because we thought it would never happen."

The case created a flurry of legislative moves at national and state level to bar recognition of legalised gay marriages in other states to save states not sanctioning such unions from having to pay benefits afforded to heterosexual couples.

Earlier this year President Bill Clinton signed into law the "Defense of Marriage" act, prohibiting federal agencies from giving spouses in same-sex marriages the same benefits as those received by heterosexual couples.

According to statistics compiled by the New York-based Lambda Legal Defence and Education Fund, 15 states have passed legislation barring homosexual couples legally married in other states from receiving benefits in their states.

These benefits include Social Security and Medicare, joint insurance for health, home, travel and cars, family leave to take care of a sick partner, hospital visitation rights, the right to will property and money to a partner and the ability to file a joint tax return, among others.
But according to Lambda, 14 mainland states were considering legalising same-sex marriages while 17 state legislatures have thrown out anti-gay marriage bills.
Robert Knight of the Washington-based Family Research Council, a group opposed to legal gay marriages, said Chang's ruling "ushered in a new era of lawlessness."
He predicted that the Hawaiian ruling would prompt more state lawmakers to bar gay marriages and deny gays married in other states any benefits in their states.
